message.content:
Below is everything you’ll need to pull **the first 25 “resolution” entries** for the IP `67.89.0.1` from VirusTotal’s public API.  
(If you’re already familiar with `curl`, skip straight to the *Command‑line* section.)

---

## 1️⃣ What “Resolutions” Means  

In VirusTotal terminology a *resolution* record represents one time the IP was seen resolving to a domain name during a scan. Each entry contains:

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `hostname` | Domain name that pointed at this IP |
| `resolved_at` | Timestamp when the resolver saw the mapping |
| `last_seen_at` | Most recent timestamp the same mapping has been observed |
| `first_seen_at` | Earliest observation of this mapping |

These are returned under the top‑level key `"data"` – each element is a single resolution object.

---

## 2️⃣ Endpoint & Parameters  

```
GET /api/v3/ip_addresses/<IP>/resolutions
Host : www.virustotal.com
Query Params :
    limit   – maximum number of items per page (max 100)
    offset  – optional start index (default 0) – useful only if you want more than 100
```

For your request:

```text
https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/ip_addresses/67.89.0.1/resolutions?limit=25
```

> ⚠️ If you later hit the pagination cursor (`next_page.cursor`) you can continue fetching subsequent pages.

---

## 3️⃣ Authentication Header  

VirusTotal uses a simple bearer‑style header:

```http
x-apikey: <YOUR_API_KEY>
```

Your key: **`sec_key5`**

---

## 4️⃣ Quick Ways To Call It

### A. Command Line (curl)

```bash
curl \
  --request GET \
  --url "https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/ip_addresses/67.89.0.1/resolutions?limit=25" \
  --header "x-apikey: sec_key5"
```

#### Expected Output Skeleton

```json
{
  "id": "67.89.0.1",
  "links": { /* … */ },
  "meta": {
      "page_size": 25,
      "total_count": 12345,
      "cursor": null
  },
  "data": [
     {
        "resource_type":"ipv4_resolved_ip",
        "attributes":{
           "hostname":"example.com",
           "resolved_at":"2024-04-01T12:34:56Z",
           "last_seen_at":"2024-04-10T08:20:00Z",
           "first_seen_at":"2024-03-28T09:11:22Z"
        }
     },
     ...
  ]
}
```

### B. One‑liner PowerShell

```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod `
  -Uri "https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/ip_addresses/67.89.0.1/resolutions?limit=25" `
  -Headers @{ "x-apikey"="sec_key5" } `
  -Method Get
```

### C. Python Script (requests library)

```python
import requests

API_URL = ("https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/"
           "ip_addresses/67.89.0.1/resolutions")
HEADERS = {"x-apikey": "sec_key5"}
PARAMS = {"limit": 25}

resp = requests.get(API_URL, headers=HEADERS, params=PARAMS)
resp.raise_for_status()          # will raise HTTPError on bad status codes
results = resp.json()

for res in results["data"]:
    attrs = res["attributes"]
    print(f"{attrs['hostname']} -> "
          f"{attrs['resolved_at']}, "
          f"seen until {attrs['last_seen_at']}")
```

Make sure you have `pip install requests` before running.

---

## 5️⃣ Things to Keep In Mind

| Topic | Notes |
|------|--------|
| **Rate Limits** | Free tier → ~4 req/minute. Paid tiers higher. |
| **Pagination** | After 25 rows you may still see many more. Look for `meta.next_page.cursor`. Pass it back as `cursor=<value>` to keep pulling. |
| **Data Retention** | VirusTotal keeps historical data for up to 90 days (or longer depending on plan). |
| **Privacy** | Do NOT share your API key publicly. Treat it like a password. |

---

## 6️⃣ Next Steps

1. Run the chosen method above.  
2. Inspect the JSON payload—especially the `data[]` array.  
3. If you need all records beyond 25, iterate over the pagination cursor until `meta.total_count` matches what you’ve collected.

Happy hunting! 🚀
